topicName: React Native Architecture Overview: Old vs. New Architecture (Fabric, TurboModules, JSI)
content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"React Native Architecture Overview: Old vs. New Architecture (Fabric, TurboModules, JSI)"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"React Native has undergone a massive architectural overhaul to address performance bottlenecks, particularly in communication between JavaScript and native host platforms. This tutorial explores the shift from the legacy architecture to the new architecture, focusing on the JavaScript Interface (JSI), TurboModules, and the Fabric renderer."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"The Legacy Architecture and Its Bottlenecks"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"In the old architecture, React Native relies on the asynchronous \"Bridge\" to facilitate communication between the JavaScript thread and the native (iOS/Android) thread. Messages must be serialized into JSON, sent across the bridge, and deserialized on the receiving end. This asynchronous and serialized nature introduces several key limitations:"},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Bridge Congestion: High-frequency events like gestures, scroll position updates, and animations cause queues to back up, leading to dropped frames and UI stutter."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Unnecessary Copying: Data passed across the bridge is frequently copied, increasing memory allocation and garbage collection overhead."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Lazy Loading Limitations: All native modules must be instantiated up front when the application starts, increasing time-to-interactive (TTI)."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"The New Architecture: Core Pillars"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"The new React Native architecture eliminates the asynchronous bridge by introducing three core pillars: JSI (JavaScript Interface), TurboModules, and Fabric. These components work together to enable synchronous execution, direct memory sharing, and improved rendering pipelines."},{"order":10,"type":"subheading","text":"1. The JavaScript Interface (JSI)"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"The JSI is a C++ layer that acts as a lightweight interface, allowing JavaScript to hold references to C++ host objects and invoke methods directly. Thanks to the JSI, JS can now call native methods synchronously without serialization. C++ objects can be exposed to JS directly, allowing pointer sharing."},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"2. TurboModules"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"TurboModules build on top of the JSI to replace the old Native Modules system. In the legacy architecture, modules like Geolocation or AsyncStorage had to be initialized immediately upon app startup. TurboModules allow for lazy loading. A native module is only instantiated when JavaScript explicitly requests it, dramatically reducing app startup times."},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Fabric Renderer"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"Fabric is the new concurrent React-based rendering system. It changes how the shadow tree is constructed. In the old architecture, a JSON representation of the UI tree was sent across the bridge to create a shadow tree on the native side. With Fabric, C++ shadow trees are shared directly between JS and native threads via the JSI, allowing high-priority updates (like animations) to interrupt low-priority layout calculations."},{"order":16,"type":"subheading","text":"Comparing Old vs. New Architecture"},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Communication: Old uses Asynchronous, Serialized Bridge. New uses Synchronous direct calls via JSI."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Module Loading: Old eagerly loads all native modules at startup. New lazily loads modules via TurboModules."},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"UI Rendering: Old uses shadow tree synchronization across the bridge. New uses shared C++ Fabric shadow trees."},{"order":20,"type":"subheading","text":"Enabling the New Architecture in Code"},{"order":21,"type":"paragraph","text":"To enable the new architecture in a modern React Native project, you typically configure flag properties in your gradle.properties file for Android and run a pod install command with environment variables for iOS."},{"order":22,"type":"code","text":"# android/gradle.properties\nnewArchEnabled=true"},{"order":23,"type":"code","text":"# ios directory terminal execution\nRCT_NEW_ARCH_ENABLED=1 bundle exec pod install"},{"order":24,"type":"paragraph","text":"By adopting JSI, TurboModules, and Fabric, React Native bridges the performance gap between cross-platform frameworks and native applications, unlocking smoother animations, faster startup times, and direct platform integrations."}]
